comparisons.peer_topic: Goodwill Impairment Testing Methodology and Results
comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporation performs qualitative assessments to determine if fair value is likely below carrying value, with an option to bypass this and proceed directly to quantitative testing; if quantitative tests show carrying value exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized for the excess of allocated equity over fair value, limited to the assigned goodwill amount, with no subsequent reversals permitted.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC describe a two-step methodology for goodwill impairment involving a preliminary qualitative assessment followed by a quantitative test if necessary. Both firms state that if the qualitative assessment indicates it is more likely than not that fair value is less than carrying value, a quantitative test is performed. Both disclose that if the reporting unit's fair value exceeds its carrying value in the quantitative test, no impairment is recognized. BAC explicitly mentions an unconditional option to bypass the qualitative assessment to proceed directly to the quantitative test, whereas GS describes the qualitative assessment as the first step without explicitly mentioning a bypass option in this excerpt.

sentences.text: Goodwill is assessed for impairment annually in the fourth quarter or more frequently if events occur or circumstances change that indicate an impairment may exist.

When assessing goodwill for impairment, first, a qualitative assessment can be made to determine whether it is more likely than not that the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value.
The quantitative goodwill test compares the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value (including goodwill and identifiable intangible assets).
If the reporting unit's estimated fair value exceeds its carrying value, goodwill is not impaired.

In performing its goodwill impairment testing, the Corporation first assesses qualitative factors to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value.
If the Corporation concludes it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value, a quantitative assessment is performed.
The Corporation has an unconditional option to bypass the qualitative assessment for any reporting unit in any period and proceed directly to performing the quantitative goodwill impairment test.
When performing the quantitative assessment, if the fair value of the reporting unit exceeds its carrying value, goodwill of the reporting unit would not be considered impaired.

comparisons.peer_topic: Qualitative Assessment Option for Goodwill Impairment
comparisons.peer_summary: The company may assess qualitative factors to determine if further quantitative testing is necessary; if it is not more-likely-than-not that fair value is less than carrying amount, no further testing is required. The company also has an unconditional option to bypass qualitative assessment and proceed directly to the quantitative test in any period.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and C disclose the option to perform a qualitative assessment before a quantitative test for goodwill impairment. Both state that if the qualitative assessment determines it is not more-likely-than-not that fair value is less than carrying value, no further testing is required. Conversely, both indicate that if it is more-likely-than-not that fair value is less than carrying value, a quantitative test must be performed. C explicitly states it has an unconditional option to bypass the qualitative assessment and proceed directly to the quantitative test, while GS outlines the qualitative assessment as the initial step.

sentences.text: Goodwill is assessed for impairment annually in the fourth quarter or more frequently if events occur or circumstances change that indicate an impairment may exist.

When assessing goodwill for impairment, first, a qualitative assessment can be made to determine whether it is more likely than not that the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value.
The Company has an option to assess qualitative factors to determine if it is necessary to perform the goodwill impairment test.

If, after assessing the totality of events or circumstances, the Company determines that it is not more-likely-than-not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount, no further testing is necessary.
The Company has an unconditional option to bypass the qualitative assessment for any reporting unit in any reporting period and proceed directly to the quantitative test.

comparisons.peer_summary: The quantitative test compares the fair value of a reporting unit to its carrying value, including goodwill. If fair value exceeds carrying value, no impairment is recognized; if carrying value exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized equal to the excess, limited to the total goodwill allocated to that unit.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and C describe the quantitative test for goodwill impairment as comparing the fair value of a reporting unit to its carrying value (including goodwill). Both firms agree that if the fair value exceeds the carrying value, the goodwill is considered not impaired. They also both indicate that an impairment loss is recognized if the carrying value exceeds the fair value. C specifies that the loss is limited to the total goodwill allocated to the reporting unit, whereas GS notes the impairment is included in depreciation and amortization.

sentences.text: The quantitative goodwill test compares the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value (including goodwill and identifiable intangible assets).
If the reporting unit's estimated fair value exceeds its carrying value, goodwill is not impaired.
An impairment is recognized if the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value and any such impairment is included in depreciation and amortization.
The quantitative test requires a comparison of the fair value of an individual reporting unit to its carrying value, including goodwill.
If the fair value of a reporting unit is in excess of the carrying value, the related goodwill is considered not impaired and no further analysis is necessary.

If the carrying value of a reporting unit exceeds the fair value, an impairment loss is recognized in an amount equal to that excess, limited to the total amount of goodwill allocated to that reporting unit.

comparisons.peer_summary: The goodwill impairment test compares the fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value, using allocated capital plus goodwill as a proxy for equity carrying values, and determines impairment if fair value is less than carrying value.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and JPM describe the goodwill impairment test as comparing the fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value. Both firms conclude that if the fair value exceeds the carrying value, the goodwill is not impaired. If the fair value is less than the carrying value, both recognize an impairment loss. JPM specifies that the impairment is recognized for the amount by which the carrying value exceeds fair value, up to the amount of goodwill allocated to the reporting unit. JPM also details using allocated capital plus goodwill as a proxy for carrying values, a specific methodological detail not present in the GS excerpt.

sentences.text: The quantitative goodwill test compares the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value (including goodwill and identifiable intangible assets).
If the reporting unit's estimated fair value exceeds its carrying value, goodwill is not impaired.
An impairment is recognized if the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value and any such impairment is included in depreciation and amortization.
The goodwill impairment test is generally performed by comparing the current fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value.
If the fair value is in excess of the carrying value, then the reporting unit's goodwill is considered not to be impaired.

If the fair value is less than the carrying value, then an impairment is recognized for the amount by which the reporting unit's carrying value exceeds its fair value, up to the amount of goodwill allocated to that reporting unit.

comparisons.peer_topic: Goodwill and Indefinite-Lived Intangible Assets Impairment Testing Methodology
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm tests goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets for impairment annually and on an interim basis when events occur. For goodwill, testing is performed at the reporting unit level, while indefinite-lived intangible assets are tested at the aggregate level of management contracts. The Firm may use a qualitative assessment or a quantitative test; if quantitative, impairment is recognized if fair value is less than carrying amount, limited to the asset's carrying amount.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and MS disclose that the firm has the option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative impairment test is necessary. Both state that if the qualitative assessment determines it is more likely than not that fair value is less than carrying value, the quantitative test is performed. In the quantitative test, both firms compare the fair value of the reporting unit with its carrying amount. Both agree that if fair value is less than carrying amount, an impairment loss is recognized equal to the excess, limited to the carrying amount of goodwill.

sentences.text: When assessing goodwill for impairment, first, a qualitative assessment can be made to determine whether it is more likely than not that the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value.
The quantitative goodwill test compares the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with its carrying value (including goodwill and identifiable intangible assets).
An impairment is recognized if the estimated fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying value and any such impairment is included in depreciation and amortization.

For both the annual and interim tests, the Firm has the option to either (i) perform a quantitative impairment test or (ii) first perform a qualitative assessment to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value is less than its carrying amount, in which case, the quantitative test would be performed.
When performing a quantitative impairment test of goodwill, the Firm compares the fair value of the reporting unit with the carrying amount.

If the fair value is less than the carrying amount, the impairment loss is equal to the excess of the carrying value over the fair value, limited to the carrying amount of goodwill within the reporting unit.
